messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan was nineteen, a fresh‑licensed fast‑food crew member who had just started his first shift at the local diner after graduating high school. The day he was in the school gymnasium during a sudden tornado, a chain of rapid, crushing events unfolded. The ceiling above the gym cracked like a dry twig; wind howled like a freight train, and a piece of the roof collapsed onto the floor, sending a shower of dust and broken boards across the field of the gym. Ethan was on the third floor, in a classroom that had been used as a shelter, and the collapse sent him tumbling into a puddle of water and debris. He was pinned under a fallen locker, his chest pressed tight enough to choke him, and he could taste the bitter iron of blood in his mouth. When the tornado finally cleared, the air was thick with the scent of hot metal and wet concrete. He had spent twenty minutes trapped, feeling his body convulse and his heart hammer against his ribs, a terrifying memory that he could still feel in the present. The horror of that night had left Ethan with a bleak conviction that he was irrevocably changed. He had come to believe that the person he had become is unrecognisable to him, that his once‑joyful laughter had been replaced by a constant gloom, and that the damage he sustained would forever shadow every corner of his life. These negative appraisals seeped into his daily routine, prompting him to rehearse what he would say before any conversation and to avoid any situation that might stir a stress reaction. Whenever he saw a co‑worker’s smile, he rehearsed a script of neutral words, certain that a slip would remind him of his failure to cope. Simultaneously, the negative appraisal that the event had left permanent scars sharpened the images that flooded his mind. When he was alone at night, he would relive the exact angle of the falling locker, the crackle of wind outside the gym walls, and the scent of hot concrete that lingers like a ghost. The terror on recall returned with the same intensity, while the smell of dust would seep into his thoughts at the slightest wind. In the same breath, his negative appraisal fed his memory, and his memory, in turn, intensified his negative appraisal, locking him into a cycle that seemed impossible to escape. At the diner, the hum of the refrigerator, the click of the cash register, and the hiss of the fryer all served as subtle triggers. Ethan would stand by the front counter during rush hour, listening to the clatter of silverware and the low murmur of customers, and feel a surge of dread as if a storm were approaching. In these moments, he suppressed thoughts about the disaster, forcing his mind to focus on the mundane task of flipping burgers. Yet the attempt to push away memories only made the images sharper; he could still see the cracked ceiling and smell the damp concrete. The suppression did not erase the terror; instead, each time he forced his mind away, the memory seemed to climb higher in his awareness. He had come to believe that he was a victim of a permanent change, and this belief fed his avoidance strategies. He avoided stepping into the parking lot during storms, refusing to drive at night, and often left his shifts early to stay indoors. The routine avoidance reinforced his conviction that the world was unsafe, that he could not trust the environment to keep him safe, and that his sense of self had been forever altered. For months, Ethan’s avoidance grew more entrenched. He would rehearse conversations not just before interactions, but before every small decision—what to say to a customer, how to order a shift, how to explain a late arrival to his supervisor. Each rehearsal was a rehearsal of his perceived inadequacy; he felt the weight of every misstep as a testament to his brokenness. The rehearsal, in turn, deepened his negative appraisal: the more he believed he had failed, the more he convinced himself that he had lost his former happiness. When he could no longer find the motivation to finish a task, he would suppress the memories and instead immerse himself in the hum of the fryers, hoping the noise would drown out the echo of the storm. Yet each attempt to suppress only brought the images back with even more force, reinforcing his belief that his trauma had permanently damaged him. The day he finally reached out for help was after a particularly chaotic shift. A customer had a sudden flare of anger and began yelling at Ethan, who had rehearsed his response but felt suddenly unable to stay calm. The memory of the collapsing locker surged so forcefully that he felt his heart pound and his vision blur. He realized that his entire coping routine—his rehearsals, his avoidance, his suppression—was failing him in the very environment he worked. In that instant, the fear of losing control and the hope that someone could help him break the cycle became unbearable. He now seeks therapy with the aim of untangling his memory and re‑gaining a sense of self that he once believed was lost forever. His most pressing fear is that he will never again feel the simple joy of a clean day at work, but he also hopes that, with help, he might learn to view the past as a part of him rather than a defining flaw.
